title: When the database can't keep up
teaches: Read replicas and replication lag, reading your own writes, and splitting users across databases
summary: **A replica is a copy of a database kept current by replaying its changes.** The primary takes every write and logs it; each replica reads the log and applies the same changes.
**Replicas scale reads, not writes.** Every replica must apply every write, so as the share of writes grows, each new replica adds less capacity for reads, and past a threshold adds none.
**Asynchronous replication runs behind.** The primary does not wait for replicas, so a replica's lag is usually milliseconds but can grow to seconds or minutes when it is overloaded.
**A reader can miss their own write.** Route reads to the primary for a short window after a write, or require the replica to wait until it has applied the write's position in the log.
**Promoting a replica that is behind loses writes.** With asynchronous replication, whatever the old primary had not yet sent is lost when a replica takes over.
**Splitting the data scales writes.** Each user's data lives on one of several independent clusters, so each cluster takes only its assigned users' writes.
**The shard key comes from the queries.** Splitting by user keeps a user's own pages on one cluster and makes queries across many users harder.
**A directory costs a lookup and buys freedom to move users.** A formula such as user number mod n needs no lookup but moves most users when n changes.
**Grow each design by ten times on paper.** The fix for today's bottleneck often has a ceiling, and capacity arithmetic shows where it lies.

parts.title: A diary site on one computer

blocks.text: In April 1999 Brad Fitzpatrick, then a college student, started LiveJournal so that he and his friends could keep online diaries. It ran on a single server hosting both a web server and a MySQL database. Within a few years it had millions of accounts, and Fitzpatrick and a small team spent those years keeping it running. In 2005 he gave a talk called "LiveJournal's Backend: A History of Scaling" that walked through every stage, one bottleneck at a time, and became a widely referenced account of how to scale a website.[^fitzpatrick]

Their first steps followed the progression we saw in lesson 2. When one machine ran out of capacity, the team moved the database to a dedicated server. As the web servers reached capacity, the engineers placed several of them behind a load balancer, all querying the single database. Then the database itself became the bottleneck. Every page on LiveJournal required database queries, and a single server could execute only so many queries a second, regardless of how many web servers sent requests. In this lesson, we will trace what Fitzpatrick's team built next and why each architecture eventually reached its limit.

Most queries on a diary site are reads, because users read far more journal entries than they write. To increase read throughput, engineers create copies of the database and distribute read queries across them. A **replica** is such a copy, kept up to date by applying the same changes as the original database in the same order. The original database, which processes every write, is the **primary**.[^names] In later lessons, we will encounter the same role under other names, such as the GFS master in lesson 6 and the primary copy of a chunk in lesson 7. In every case, this single node orders all state changes.

MySQL implements replication with a log. The primary appends each committed change to a file called the **binary log**. Each replica maintains a connection to the primary, reads the log as it grows, and applies each change to its own local data.[^binlog] The primary does not wait for any replica to acknowledge the change before confirming the write to the client. This mechanism is **asynchronous replication**. Write latency remains as low as on a single database, and a slow or unreachable replica does not block incoming writes.

The trade-off of asynchronous replication is that replicas always lag behind the primary. The delay between the primary committing a change and a replica applying it is the **replication lag**. On a lightly loaded system, replication lag is a few milliseconds. When a replica is overloaded, or when a single large transaction takes a long time to execute, the lag grows to seconds or even minutes.

Before adding replicas, we can calculate the capacity. Suppose the site receives 10,000 queries a second, 5% of which are writes, and each database server can process 3,000 queries a second. Read queries go to the replicas, while write queries go to the primary and must also be replayed by every replica. Each replica's load is the total write rate plus its share of the read rate, or 500 + 9,500 / n queries a second. With five replicas, each replica handles 500 + 1,900 = 2,400 queries a second, which is 80% of a server's 3,000 queries a second capacity.

blocks.caption: A primary and its read replicas at 10,000 queries a second (the dots run at a hundredth of that rate, in slow motion). Each replica's bar shows its utilisation, and the number under it shows its replication lag behind the primary. Tap the primary to fail it.
blocks.task: Raise the share of writes until the replicas fall behind, and try adding replicas to catch them up.

blocks.text: Now increase the proportion of writes. At 20% writes, each replica must apply 2,000 writes a second before serving a single read, leaving capacity for only 1,000 reads a second per replica. Serving the remaining 8,000 reads a second requires at least 8,000 / 1,000 = 8 replicas. At 30% writes, the 3,000 writes a second saturate every replica's capacity on their own, and adding more replicas provides no spare capacity for reads. When incoming queries exceed a replica's throughput, its request queue grows, and because replication events wait in that capacity bottleneck, replication lag increases continuously. If the site sends Q queries a second with a write fraction w across n replicas, each replica processes wQ writes a second plus (1 − w)Q / n reads a second, which must remain below 3,000 queries a second. Total throughput Q cannot exceed 3,000 / (w + (1 − w)/n) queries a second, which approaches a ceiling of 3,000 / w queries a second as n grows. Read replicas scale read throughput, but they do not increase write throughput.

We can apply the same arithmetic to ten times the traffic, a scale test we run on every design in this course. At 100,000 queries a second with 5% writes, the primary and every replica must each apply 5,000 writes a second, exceeding the 3,000 queries a second capacity of a single server. A design that works at 10,000 queries a second fails at 100,000 queries a second regardless of how many replicas we add. In his 2005 talk, Fitzpatrick described LiveJournal hitting this ceiling when its replicas spent most of their capacity replaying writes and had almost none left to serve reads.

In the figure above, tap the primary to fail it. Writes stop immediately. To restore write availability, you **promote** a replica, configuring it as the new primary and pointing the remaining replicas at it. With asynchronous replication, any transaction the old primary committed but did not yet transmit is missing from every replica and is permanently lost, even though the client received a success response. The greater the replication lag, the more committed writes are lost. **Synchronous replication**, in which the primary waits for replicas to acknowledge a write before replying to the client, prevents data loss at the cost of higher write latency. Waiting for every replica makes each write as slow as the slowest replica, so many engineers configure the primary to wait for just one replica.[^semisync] When an operator performs a manual failover, they follow four steps: verify that the primary is unreachable across several consecutive health checks; fence off the old primary from the web servers so it cannot accept writes if it recovers; promote the replica with the most recent log position to minimise data loss; and reconfigure the remaining replicas and web servers to use the new primary. Automating failover safely requires distributed consensus, which we will cover in lesson 11. To monitor the replication lag that determines how much data is at risk during a failover, an engineer can configure the primary to update a single timestamp row once a second; on any replica, the difference between the current clock time and that stored timestamp measures its lag.

Replication lag also causes consistency bugs during normal operation. Suppose you post a comment, receive confirmation that it is saved, reload the page, and find the comment missing. The write succeeded on the primary, but the reload routed your read query to a replica that had not yet applied the change. No data was lost, and reloading again a moment later displays the comment, but to the author the system appears broken.

blocks.caption: Messages over time, running down the page: a client posts a comment, then reloads the page 150 ms later. Writes are in orange, and reads are in blue. The replica's lag is kept short in the diagram so the sequence fits; under high load, lag can reach several seconds.
blocks.task: With a lag long enough to lose the comment, try both fixes (Primary for 10 s, Wait for my write) and play each through.

blocks.text: To prevent this anomaly, engineers implement **read-your-writes** consistency, which guarantees that a user always sees their own updates even if other users see them slightly later. Two implementations are standard. In the simpler approach, the application records the timestamp of the user's last write in their session and routes their read queries to the primary for a fixed window, such as 10 seconds; this adds a small amount of read load to the primary for active writers. In the more exact approach, the primary returns the binary log position of the write to the client, and subsequent reads pass this position to a replica, which waits until it has replayed the log up to that point before executing the read query.[^position] This second method guarantees that the user sees their write without adding read load to the primary, though a read request will block if the replica is lagging.

Neither method makes replicas up to date for other users. A friend loading your journal from another replica may still miss the new comment for a second or two. For most applications this delay is acceptable, provided engineers choose that consistency trade-off explicitly for each type of query rather than discovering it through user bug reports. In lesson 13, we will classify these consistency guarantees and their latency costs.

Because read replicas could not increase LiveJournal's write capacity, Fitzpatrick's team had to partition the writes across multiple primaries. They divided users into groups and assigned each group to its own independent **cluster**, consisting of one primary and one or two replicas, which stored all records for those users: journal entries, comments and account settings. Because a user's writes went only to their assigned cluster, each cluster processed only a fraction of the site's total write traffic. Partitioning a database this way is called **sharding**, each partition is a **shard**, and the column used to assign a row to a shard is the **shard key**. LiveJournal used the user ID as its shard key.

blocks.caption: 8,000 writes a second partitioned by user across independent clusters, each with a capacity of 3,000 queries a second. A directory maps each user to their assigned cluster. Slow motion, at a hundredth of the rate.
blocks.task: Add clusters until each one is under 80% busy.

blocks.text: Your choice of shard key determines which queries remain fast. When you shard by user ID, all the data required to render a single user's journal resides on one cluster, so the web server needs only one query to one database. However, rendering a page that aggregates entries from many users, such as a friends feed showing the latest posts from everyone you follow, requires the web server to query multiple clusters and merge the results in application code. You should select a shard key by measuring your query rates and choosing the attribute that keeps the most frequent queries within a single shard. Even then, skewed access patterns can create bottlenecks, because a cluster assigned a celebrity user with high traffic will experience higher load than the others.

To route queries to the right cluster, LiveJournal maintained a small global database called a **directory** that mapped each user ID to a cluster number, which web servers queried and cached in memory. An alternative routing method computes the shard directly from the key using a modulo formula, such as `user_id mod num_clusters`, which requires no database lookup. The drawback of modulo routing appears when you add capacity. Increasing the cluster count from 3 to 4 with `user_id mod n` reassigns 75% of users to a different cluster, requiring you to migrate most of the dataset before the new cluster can serve traffic. With a directory, you can route new sign-ups to the new cluster immediately and migrate existing users one at a time to rebalance load without disrupting the rest. In lesson 5, we will encounter the same routing problem in distributed caches and solve it using consistent hashing.

parts.title: The simplest fix for the current bottleneck

blocks.text: At each stage of LiveJournal's growth, the engineers made the smallest architectural change that resolved their current bottleneck: separating the database server, adding web servers, adding read replicas, and finally sharding into user clusters. They did not over-engineer for future scale prematurely, even though each architecture had a hard throughput ceiling predictable from simple arithmetic. Building a system for 100 times your current traffic costs far more in engineering time and hardware than solving the problem in front of you, and that future traffic may never materialise. Capacity arithmetic instead gives you lead time: calculate what breaks when traffic grows by a factor of 10, identify the next bottleneck, and build the replacement before utilization reaches 100%.

Sharding by user introduced operational complexity that LiveJournal's engineers managed for years. Every query had to look up a user's cluster ID first. Cross-user queries required scatter-gather requests across multiple shards and an in-memory merge. Rebalancing load by migrating a user between clusters required a multi-step tool: copy the user's historical rows to the destination cluster while the source cluster continues handling writes, briefly lock the user's account to block new writes, copy any rows modified during the initial transfer, update the directory to point to the destination cluster, and release the write lock. Furthermore, an update affecting two users on different clusters could no longer execute inside a single ACID database transaction; if one cluster committed and the other aborted, the database could not roll back the first commit automatically, forcing engineers either to avoid cross-shard writes, co-locate related data on the same shard, or implement multi-step coordination in application code. Every shard also had its own primary that could fail. LiveJournal's next major bottleneck, however, was neither write throughput nor failover. Even across sharded clusters, popular journal entries were being queried from disk thousands of times a second, so in 2003 Fitzpatrick built an in-memory caching layer that was far cheaper than buying more database servers. We will design that system in lesson 5.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Each replica's load = all the writes + its share of the reads.
Lag is the price of asynchronous replication; it grows when a replica is overloaded.
Sharding divides writes; the shard key decides which queries stay on one machine.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on copies and splits
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A database gets 10,000 queries a second, 30% of them writes, and each server can do 3,000 queries a second. Why will adding read replicas not help?
choices: Each replica must apply all 3,000 writes a second, which fills it
The load balancer in front of the replicas becomes the bottleneck at around six replicas
Replication lag grows with the number of replicas, so reads become too stale to use
items.why: Every replica applies every write. At 3,000 writes a second each replica is saturated by writes alone, so adding a new replica adds no capacity for reads. Scaling write throughput requires sharding.

items.ask: A user posts a comment, reloads, and the comment is missing; a moment later it appears. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The primary lost the write and a retry from the web server put it back
The reload read from a replica that had not yet applied the write
The browser showed a cached copy of the page from before the comment
items.why: With asynchronous replication a replica runs slightly behind the primary. The write was committed on the primary, but the subsequent read was routed to a replica that had not yet replayed it.

items.ask: Which fix gives a user read-your-writes without adding any read load to the primary?
choices: Send all of a user's reads to the primary for 10 seconds after each write they make
Return the write's log position, and have later reads wait until the replica has applied it
Switch replication to synchronous, so every replica confirms each write before it is saved
items.why: Passing the log position allows any replica to serve a consistent read once it has replayed the log up to that point, without sending extra read queries to the primary. Routing reads to the primary works but increases primary load, while synchronous replication increases latency for every write.

items.ask: With asynchronous replication, the primary fails and a replica 3 seconds behind is promoted. What happens to the committed writes that had not yet reached that replica?
choices: It replays them from the binary log it received
They are lost: the new primary never received them
They wait in the load balancer's queue and are sent on later
items.why: Those transactions were committed only on the old primary and were never transmitted to the replica. Promoting the lagging replica loses those writes; preventing this loss requires synchronous replication, which increases write latency.

items.ask: A site shards by user. Which query becomes harder than it was on one database?
choices: Showing one user's own journal entries, newest first
Saving a new entry written by one user
The latest entries of everyone a user follows
items.why: The accounts a user follows are distributed across many shards, so building the feed requires querying multiple shards and merging the results. A single user's own reads and writes remain on one shard.

items.ask: Why might a sharded system keep a directory of which shard holds each user instead of computing user number mod the number of shards?
choices: With mod, adding a shard moves most users; a directory moves only those you choose
With mod, the shard for a user cannot be computed until the database has been asked first
A directory spreads users more evenly than mod, which always puts more users on the first shard
items.why: Increasing the shard count from n to n + 1 with modulo hashing changes the assigned shard for roughly n out of every n + 1 users. A directory requires a lookup, which web servers cache in memory, and allows engineers to migrate users individually.

items.ask: A service runs 2,000 queries a second, 20% of them writes, on a primary and two replicas that can each do 3,000 queries a second. It expects ten times the traffic. What does the arithmetic say?
choices: Add replicas in proportion: about 20 replicas will carry 20,000 queries a second
Nothing needs to change yet, because the three servers are each less than half busy
At 4,000 writes a second no single server can keep up, so the writes must be split
items.why: At ten times the traffic, the system receives 4,000 writes a second. Because the primary and every replica must apply all 4,000 writes a second and each server can execute only 3,000 queries a second, no number of read replicas can handle the load; engineers must partition the writes across shards.

fitzpatrick.title: Danga's tools
fitzpatrick.text: Fitzpatrick's company, Danga Interactive, wrote much of the infrastructure software LiveJournal needed and released it as open source: memcached (covered in lesson 5), the load balancer Perlbal, the distributed file store MogileFS and the job queue Gearman. Six Apart acquired LiveJournal and Danga Interactive in January 2005.

names.title: Names for the copies
names.text: MySQL's documentation called the primary the master and the replicas slaves until July 2020, and older engineering literature uses those terms. Other distributed systems use the terms leader and follower, which we will use in lesson 11 for systems where nodes run a consensus protocol to elect their own leader.

binlog.title: What the log holds
binlog.text: Early versions of MySQL replication logged each SQL statement (such as "UPDATE entries SET ...") and replicas re-executed the statement. Non-deterministic statements whose output depends on wall-clock time or randomness, such as queries calling NOW() or RAND(), can evaluate to different values on a replica, so MySQL 5.1 introduced row-based replication to log the modified row values directly.

semisync.title: Halfway
semisync.text: Many systems configure the primary to wait for an acknowledgement from just one replica, rather than all of them, before confirming a write to the client. MySQL calls this semi-synchronous replication. A committed write is then guaranteed to exist on at least two machines if the primary fails, while write latency increases by only the network round trip to the fastest replica rather than the slowest.

position.title: Waiting for a position
position.text: MySQL provides built-in SQL functions that block until a replica has replayed the binary log up to a specified coordinate (`MASTER_POS_WAIT`, and in newer releases `WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET` using global transaction IDs). Before running a read query, the web server calls this function with the log coordinate returned by the user's last write, ensuring the replica's response includes that write.
